one_liner: Memory-safe Rust TLS 1.2/1.3 library on AWS-LC crypto; beats OpenSSL 3.6.1 per core on handshakes, resumption and AES-GCM bulk.
what_it_does: rustls is a TLS 1.2 and 1.3 client and server library written in Rust with #![forbid(unsafe_code)] and no network I/O of its own. ClientConnection and ServerConnection are state machines: they turn received TLS bytes into plaintext and plaintext into TLS bytes in caller-owned buffers, and you drive the socket yourself or through tokio-rustls. All cryptography comes from a pluggable CryptoProvider, either rustls-aws-lc-rs (recommended) or rustls-ring. It does not have an OpenSSL API: C and C++ callers use the rustls-ffi C API, or the experimental rustls-libssl shim, which implements part of the OpenSSL 3 libssl ABI for curl and nginx.
how_it_is_fast: Primitive speed comes from AWS-LC through aws-lc-rs: its AVX-512F/VAES AES-GCM and AVX-512IFMA RSA (both contributed by Intel) explain the x86 bulk and server-RSA results. On ARM64, BoringSSL, AWS-LC and OpenSSL all run AES-256-GCM at 2264-2268 MB/s, so the lead over OpenSSL comes from the protocol layer. That layer is a sans-I/O design over caller buffers with a write-through "unbuffered" API, about 13 KiB per session against OpenSSL's 69 KiB. Tuning includes removing a receive-path memmove (PR #2155), packing several handshake messages into one record (#2041) and a cheaper extension representation (0.23.31). For many cores, configs are shared read-only in an Arc, and ticket-key rotation switched from a Mutex to a RwLock (TicketRotator, PR #2193, 0.23.17), which removes the lock contention the maintainers measured in OpenSSL 3.0/3.4. The reports do not name the component behind the handshake lead.
when_to_use: Rust services that open or accept many TLS connections: per core on x86, full handshakes are 1.32-2.59x and resumptions 1.87-3.20x faster than OpenSSL 3.6.1

Many-core servers (80-core Ampere Altra tested): full TLS 1.3 handshakes and ticket resumption scale per thread with the tightest latency distribution of rustls, BoringSSL and OpenSSL 3.0/3.4. Use 0.23.17 or later
Servers that hold many concurrent sessions: 10,000 TLS 1.3 sessions peaked at 131,816 KiB against OpenSSL's 688,436 KiB (2023 run)
AES-GCM bulk transfer on AVX-512 x86 with the aws-lc-rs provider: 1.11-1.27x of OpenSSL 3.6.1 send/receive MB/s
ARM64 handshake-heavy loads: on an Ampere Altra, rustls 0.23.15 did 1.9-3.5x the full and resumed handshakes of OpenSSL 3.3.2
when_not_to_use: ChaCha20-Poly1305 bulk traffic: in the 2023 run rustls reached only 0.56-0.58x of OpenSSL 3.2.0 on AVX-512, because AWS-LC lacked OpenSSL's AVX-512 ChaCha path. The 2026 report drops the ChaCha row, although admin/bench-measure.mk still runs it
Bulk-throughput-bound ARM64 servers: on Ampere Altra (2024), rustls moved 0.93-1.04x of OpenSSL 3.3.2's MB/s. On x86, BoringSSL still sends faster (8,291.9 vs 8,133.85 MB/s, TLS 1.2 AES-128-GCM)

C/C++ code that needs an OpenSSL drop-in: rustls-libssl is experimental, covers only the libssl subset used by curl and nginx, and still needs OpenSSL's libcrypto. rustls-ffi has its own C API, gives no ABI-stability guarantee and recommends static linking

Protocols or features it refuses or lacks: TLS 1.0/1.1, SSLv3, renegotiation, finite-field DHE, custom extensions (SSL_CTX_add_custom_ext), DTLS (issue #40 open), server-side ECH, and deferred or async private-key operations (roadmap item #850)

High-churn servers with session-ID resumption on the default cache: ServerSessionMemoryCache is a Mutex around a HashMap and VecDeque. One quinn server spent 11% of accept-thread time in take() (#2972). The maintainers expect demanding users to supply their own store

integration.form: crate (Rust); C static or shared library via rustls-ffi; experimental libssl.so.3 shim via rustls-libssl
integration.dependencies: rustls itself: subtle, zeroize, rustls-pki-types, optional tracing and rustls-webpki (default) and optional brotli or zlib-rs for certificate compression. A crypto provider crate is required: rustls-aws-lc-rs (needs a C/C++ compiler to build aws-lc-sys, plus CMake and Go for FIPS) or rustls-ring. The benchmark binary also links tikv-jemallocator
integration.min_toolchain: Stable 0.23.x: Rust 1.71 (rust-version on crates.io). 0.24.0-dev on main: Rust 1.85, edition 2024. Add a C/C++ compiler for the aws-lc-rs provider; rustls-ffi needs Rust 1.73+ and cargo-c
integration.platforms: The rustls core is platform-independent and no_std-capable. Real reach depends on the provider: aws-lc-rs runs on targets that both AWS-LC and Rust std support, and ring builds on more targets. Published benchmarks cover x86-64 (Xeon E-2386G, AVX-512) and aarch64 (Ampere Altra)
integration.thread_safety: ClientConfig and ServerConfig are Send + Sync and meant to be shared in an Arc, one per process. ServerConnection is Send + Sync (docs.rs auto traits), but its methods take &mut self, so one thread drives a connection at a time
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — not for Rust or C code written against the OpenSSL API, which needs rewriting to the rustls or rustls-ffi API. rustls-libssl can stand in for libssl.so.3 under curl and nginx on some Ubuntu and Fedora releases, but it is experimental and keeps OpenSSL's libcrypto

gotchas: The published numbers come from a benchmark binary with jemalloc as its global allocator. In the 2023 run, glibc malloc cut rustls+aws-lc send throughput 2.2-2.4x (2,847 vs 6,712 MB/s) because of page faults. Benchmark your own allocator

The benchmark is in-memory client-to-server with no sockets or syscalls. Since 0.23.31, TLS 1.3 uses X25519MLKEM768 by default, which cut rustls TLS 1.3 RSA client full handshakes 1.62x from 0.23.15 and sends larger messages

API churn: from 0.24 you must pass a CryptoProvider explicitly, the providers move out into separate crates (rustls-aws-lc-rs, rustls-ring), and main has a new read_tls/MessageHandler I/O API. Stable is still 0.23.x

Pin 0.23.45 or later. RUSTSEC-2026-0285 affects 0.23.13 through 0.23.44: TLS 1.3 handshake messages were accepted across key changes. The benchmarked 0.23.37 is affected. Earlier advisories: RUSTSEC-2024-0399 (panic in Acceptor::accept on a fragmented ClientHello, 0.23.13-0.23.17) and RUSTSEC-2024-0336 (complete_io infinite loop, before 0.23.5)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: aws-lc-rs, ring and Graviola are crypto providers that plug into rustls, so they are not alternatives to it; aws-lc-rs is the default and the one benchmarked. Pick rustls over AWS-LC, wolfSSL, Fizz or picotls when you want a memory-safe TLS 1.2+1.3 stack in Rust (or through rustls-ffi) with top per-core handshake numbers. Pick those C/C++ libraries when you need an OpenSSL-style C API, and pick ztls only for Zig TLS 1.3 code that is bound by per-record latency.
verified_claims_summary: The rustls maintainers ran single-threaded, in-memory client/server benchmarks on 2026-03-07. The machine was a bare-metal Xeon E-2386G (AVX-512, HT and frequency scaling off) on Debian 12. They compared rustls 0.23.37 with aws-lc-rs 1.16.0 (Rust 1.94.0) against OpenSSL 3.6.1 (default ./Configure; make, GCC 12.2 toolchain) driven by ctz/openssl-bench 82b86b22. rustls led on all 16 rows: AES-GCM bulk 1.11-1.27x, full handshakes 1.32-2.59x, resumptions 1.87-3.20x. The December 2023 run (0.22.0 vs 3.2.0) was mixed: rustls lost server RSA full handshakes (0.70-0.73x), receive throughput (0.83-0.93x) and ChaCha20 (0.56-0.58x), but used about 81% less memory at 10,000 sessions.
status_note: Very active: 0.23.45 shipped 2026-09-14 after roughly monthly 0.23.x releases, and 0.24 is in development with breaking API changes. It has about 945M crates.io downloads, a founder funded full-time through Prossimo, and a permissive Apache-2.0/MIT/ISC license.
